A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoCoT2V-Bench project. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial methodological and organizational revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of nine video-generation methods, prompt-complexity measurements, correlation analyses and qualitative examples in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of thirteen methods, human-annotation results, evaluation-method comparisons and updated supplementary analyses and examples.

M1.justification: The evaluation procedure is substantially redesigned. DeQA-based perceptual scoring replaces aesthetic/technical scoring; direct MLLM scoring and hierarchical scene-gated VQA replace description similarity and Hungarian event matching. SAM3 tracking with MLLM verification replaces event-based character-consistency extraction. HERD changes from seven-dimensional polarity-aware QA to six-dimensional auditor/evaluator scoring. Standalone content clarity disappears, while multiscale dynamic quality and streaming implementations are introduced.

E1.justification: The long-video task and eighteen themes remain, but v2 substantially revises the evaluated input requirements: descriptive prompts enriched with evaluation information become stories with identifiable characters and fixed appearance constraints across scenes (Section 3.2; Appendix D.2). The auxiliary complexity comparison adds AniMaker/TinyStories prompts, while v1's Text-to-Image-2M aesthetic-calibration corpus is no longer used.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains all nine original generators and adds StoryAdapter, SANA-Video, LongLive and LongSANA. StoryAdapter is evaluated through a Wan2.2 image-to-video adaptation. v2 also introduces explicit comparisons against QA-based and direct-scoring HERD alternatives and a character-removal background-consistency variant (Table 3 and Figure 4).

E3.justification: The evaluated prompt count changes from 240 to 234, with substantially revised metric scales, sampling and aggregation. Generated event-level comparator prompts are replaced by verified scene splits that reconstruct the original prompt verbatim; complexity scoring changes from DeepSeek-V3.1 to V3.2. New protocols include human evaluation of a random 5% of generated videos and dynamic-quality calibration on 100 disjoint annotated videos.

E4.justification: v2 adds human-alignment validation, background-masking ablation and comparisons of HERD implementations. Theme and prompt-complexity analyses are retained but revised in Appendix C; the specific event-alignment/temporal-consistency entanglement analysis from v1 Section 4.4 disappears. Appendix E replaces three pairwise examples with five cases displaying all thirteen methods.

E5.justification: v2 newly discloses generation seed 0 and three-annotator mean opinion scoring. The repeated randomized MLLM judgments described for v1's content-clarity metric disappear with that metric. These are limited changes in randomness and estimation reporting; neither version provides confidence intervals or multi-seed uncertainty for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: The main and supplementary result sets are extensively replaced and expanded. VGoT leads v1 Table 2 with an overall score of 72.17, whereas LongLive leads v2 Table 2 with 70.56 under the revised prompts and metrics; these are not comparable-setting performance changes. New results include human-alignment coefficients, such as HERD SRCC 0.5844, component comparisons, dynamic-quality scores and new qualitative cases.

T1.justification: v1's event-matching inversion penalty, transition-abruptness formulation and intra-/inter-event consistency definitions are removed. v2 introduces formal scene gates, character/facet aggregation and scene-normalized FGA equations, together with perceptual and multiscale dynamic-score definitions (Section 4; Appendix B.3). These substantially change mathematical metric definitions, although neither version presents theoretical guarantees.

C1.justification: The claimed evaluation contributions shift from event-level consistency and content clarity toward hierarchical scene alignment, character identity tracking and multiscale dynamics. Agreement with human judgments becomes an explicit main contribution. The abstract emphasizes strong background consistency versus weak character consistency, and v1's claim to the first systematic benchmark is omitted.

C2.justification: v1 interprets internal correlations as evidence that static-quality bias and metric entanglement are limited. v2 instead discusses shared semantic dependencies and associations between perceptual quality and other scores. It adds explanations for using complete frames in background evaluation, attributes weak complexity associations to restricted variance, and acknowledges a visual-style exception with a hypothesis about auditor-text hallucinations.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands prompt templates, verification instructions, baseline-adaptation details and human-annotation documentation. It newly specifies generation defaults of 16 fps and 480p with exceptions. Conversely, v1 Section 7's release URL and statement that draft prompt data are available disappear; this removes access information without establishing that the resources themselves were withdrawn.

R1.justification: The methodological positioning broadens substantially: v2 explicitly draws on DPG-Bench/FIFA for fine-grained alignment, DEVIL for multiscale dynamics and recent image-quality assessment work for perceptual scoring. StoryBench, AniMaker and newer generation methods enter the discussion. References supporting the former design, including FingER and Hungarian matching, disappear; these changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and central methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. Benchmark construction and evaluation become separate main sections, experiments are reorganized, and theme/complexity analyses move into restructured appendices. The new LoCoT2V-Eval terminology accompanies substantial narrative restructuring rather than an isolated renaming.

P2.justification: The main text switches from one to two columns, the overview is redrawn, and new evaluation-pipeline and human-validation displays are added. Table 2 gains input-format groups and different metric columns. Several radar/violin displays are replaced by bars or heatmaps, and qualitative comparisons expand into full-method grids with prompts presented separately.

improvement.justification: v1 asserts evaluation reliability without validating scores against human judgments. v2 addresses this important deficiency through a three-annotator study, component comparisons and disjoint calibration data (Table 3, Figure 4 and Appendix B), while acknowledging the HERD visual-style exception. Verified prompt splitting also strengthens experimental control. Although release information and some earlier analyses are lost, the new validation substantially strengthens the evidence supporting the paper's central contribution.
